opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a really natural progression for us. A lot of what we learned working on diffusion models for images and video carries over almost directly to language. In some sense it's the same core idea: instead of generating things one piece at a time, left to right, you start from noise, or a corrupted version of the data, and you learn to iteratively refine it into something coherent. That's worked spectacularly well for images and video, and the question we kept asking was, why should language be any different?

The big challenge is that text is discrete. With images you're in a continuous space. You can add Gaussian noise, and the math works out really cleanly with score functions and stochastic differential equations. With tokens you can't just add a little bit of noise to a word. So a lot of our work has been figuring out the right analog of those ideas in discrete spaces: how to define the corruption process, what the model should learn to predict, and how to get a training objective that's principled and actually scales. Things like learning ratios of probabilities in discrete spaces, sort of a discrete version of score matching, came directly out of thinking about what made continuous diffusion work.

Beyond the theory, there are a lot of practical lessons. In image diffusion we saw huge gains from better samplers, from distillation techniques that reduce the number of steps, and from guidance methods that let you trade off quality and diversity or steer generation. All of those have counterparts in language. One of the most exciting things about diffusion for text is speed. Because you generate many tokens in parallel and refine them over a number of steps, you're not bottlenecked by sequential, token-by-token decoding the way autoregressive models are. That's very much an inheritance from the image world, where people worked hard to get from thousands of steps down to a handful.

Video taught us a lot too, especially about structure and consistency over long sequences, and about how to handle very large outputs efficiently. Those are exactly the kinds of issues you run into when you want to generate long passages of text or code that are globally coherent.

There's also a nice flexibility you get from the diffusion view. Since the model isn't committed to strictly left-to-right generation, things like infilling, editing, and controllable generation become much more natural. In images, inpainting fell out of the framework almost for free. We're seeing the same thing in language, and I think that's going to open up some really interesting applications.

So the short answer is that the image and video work gave us both the mathematical toolkit and the intuition. The work on the language side has been about adapting those ideas to the discrete setting and showing that they can be competitive with, and in some ways better than, the autoregressive paradigm that's dominated for so long.

r001.rationale: The response says image diffusion distillation can reduce steps and that language has counterparts, but it does not identify distillation research in video diffusion as a source of acceleration ideas for language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's been a huge influence, honestly. A lot of what we're doing with diffusion language models really started from watching what happened in images and video over the last few years. If you go back to the early days of diffusion for images, the generations were kind of blurry, low resolution, nobody thought they'd compete with GANs. And then within a couple of years, with better architectures, better noise schedules, better training objectives, classifier-free guidance, all of these ingredients, suddenly it became the dominant paradigm. So one thing that gave us a lot of confidence is that we'd seen the trajectory before. When our first diffusion language models were a bit behind autoregressive models in quality, we had this intuition that the gap was going to close as the methods matured, and that's largely what's happened.

The second thing, which I think is actually the deeper point, is that the core advantage is the same across modalities. Diffusion is fundamentally a parallel generation process. In an image you're denoising all the pixels at once instead of generating them one by one, and that's exactly why it's so fast and why you can do things like inpainting, or editing a region, or conditioning on partial information. When you bring that over to text, you get the same benefits. You can generate many tokens in parallel, so inference is dramatically faster, and you can do things like fill in the middle, or revise an earlier part of the output in light of what comes later, which is awkward or impossible with a left-to-right model that commits to each token and can never go back.

Now, the challenge is that text is discrete. You can't just add Gaussian noise to a word. So a lot of our work has been about figuring out what the right analog of the noising process is for discrete data. We've found that masking-based corruption, where you progressively hide tokens and train the model to recover them, works really well, and interestingly it ends up looking a lot like BERT-style masked language modeling, just with a principled generative story on top. And then you get to borrow ideas from the continuous side, things like how to parameterize the denoiser, how to schedule the noise, how to do guidance, how to distill the sampler into fewer steps. The transfer isn't one to one, but the lineage is very clear.

And then the last piece I'd mention is on the systems side. The image and video folks have figured out a lot about how to make diffusion sampling efficient, how to trade off the number of denoising steps against quality, how to run it on hardware well. Those lessons apply pretty directly to language, and that's a big part of why we think diffusion LLMs can be both faster and cheaper to serve than autoregressive ones, which matters a lot once you start thinking about agents and applications that need many tokens quickly.

r001.rationale: The response names distilling the sampler into fewer steps among ideas transferred from continuous diffusion, then says image and video sampling-efficiency lessons apply to language and help make diffusion LLMs faster and cheaper.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot we can learn from image and video generation, although language brings some different challenges. One of the appealing things about diffusion is that you don’t have to make every decision in a fixed, left-to-right order. You can start with a rough candidate and refine it, revisiting different parts of the output. That’s been very powerful for images, and it’s an interesting capability to bring to language.

But the transfer isn’t automatic. Images are naturally represented with continuous values, whereas text is discrete. So you have to think carefully about what it means to corrupt a sentence, what the model should predict, and how to turn that prediction into a useful sampling procedure. Masking tokens gives you one way to formulate that problem.

Another important connection is efficiency. In image diffusion, a lot of effort has gone into reducing the number of refinement steps. For language, that’s particularly important because you’re competing with very strong autoregressive models. You can potentially predict many tokens in parallel, but if you need too many rounds of refinement, you lose that advantage.

So I see image and video diffusion as a source of ideas about training, sampling, and controlling generation. The research question is which of those ideas carry over, and where we need something specifically designed for language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot we can learn from image and video diffusion, both in terms of how we train these models and how we generate samples efficiently. The basic idea is similar: you start with something noisy and gradually refine it. That gives you a way to make predictions jointly and then revise them, which is quite different from generating text one token at a time and never going back.

But language introduces some important differences. Images are naturally represented as continuous quantities, whereas text is discrete, so you have to think carefully about what it means to add noise and reverse that process. You can borrow ideas from the image setting, but you can’t necessarily transfer every design choice directly.

One direction I find particularly interesting is bringing over techniques for reducing the number of sampling steps. Parallel generation is attractive, but if you need too many rounds of refinement, you can lose that advantage. So the question is how to get the benefits of iterative refinement while keeping generation efficient.

r001.rationale: The response says image and video diffusion can inspire methods for reducing sampling steps, but it does not identify distillation research as that source of ideas.
